public_rationale: The August 7, 2024 committee analysis of the July 3 version ties principal safety, testing and compliance duties to covered models (e3). July 9 commentary on that version identifies $100 million in training cost as the key threshold (e2). Together, these support the claim about much of the bill's requirements (e2, e3). The preceding July 2 committee analysis specifies initial training exceeding both $100 million at average cloud-compute prices and 10^26 operations, plus a separate fine-tuning branch (e1). This supports the qualitative inference about substantial training resources, without establishing company valuations (e1, e2).
limitations: The July 3 bill text was inaccessible; the finding relies on the relevant-version committee analysis and contemporaneous commentary, with the preceding analysis supplying threshold details.
The preceding analysis measures cost using average cloud-compute prices, not necessarily actual expenditure (e1).
Separate fine-tuning coverage prevents inferring that every covered developer must itself fund a $100 million initial training run (e1).
The evidence does not verify billion-dollar valuations, establish a company-size exemption, or rule out indirect effects on smaller firms.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Much of SB-1047's requirements are limited to models with training runs of $100 million or more, and companies that can afford such runs, presumably valued in the billions, are not exactly little tech.

statement.excerpt: But you don't make clear that much of the bill's requirements are limited to models with training runs of $100 million+. Companies that can afford that, presumably valued in the billions, are not exactly "little-tech."
statement.document_title: An open letter to Fei-Fei Li concerning California’s proposed AI regulation, SB-1047

from_speaker: models with training runs of $100 million+
our_interpretation: Assess the proposed bill current when the post appeared, rather than later amendments or its eventual disposition.
Read 'much' as the main developer safety, assessment, testing and reporting obligations, without requiring every provision to share the threshold.
Read '$100 million+' as an approximate description of the statutory training-compute cost threshold, rather than a claim about treatment of a model costing exactly $100 million.

Read the company-size sentence as a qualitative inference about the resources needed to afford such training. 'Presumably' does not firmly assert a verified billion-dollar valuation for every affected developer.
The target period covers the July 3 version through the post date. This is an observation about a pending legislative text, not a financial reporting period.
Metric scope is null because the testable monetary threshold defines legislative coverage; no named company's financial results or valuation are being measured.
criteria.support_condition: The contemporaneous bill ties its main developer obligations to covered models whose initial training exceeds approximately $100 million in compute costs, supporting the ordinary description of that training as financially substantial. Separate provisions or derivative-model rules do not by themselves defeat 'much.'
criteria.contradiction_condition: The contemporaneous bill lacks the claimed initial-training cost threshold, or its main developer obligations generally apply to independently trained models below it. Evidence that some smaller firms face indirect effects would not alone contradict the narrower wording.

evidence.excerpt:
This bill establishes requirements the developer of an artificial intelligence (AI) model trained
using a specified level of computing power (“covered model”) must meet before training and
releasing the model, establishes a state entity to provide oversight and guidance regarding
covered model compliance, provides related whistleblower protections, grants enforcement
authority to the Attorney General and Labor Commissioner, and creates CalCompute, a public
cloud computing cluster.
